findings.description: Wheel archive extracted with zipfile.extractall into app-data install image without explicit path-traversal validation of member names
findings.code_snippet:
def build_image(self):
        # 1. first extract the wheel
        LOGGER.debug("build install image for %s to %s", self._wheel.name, self._image_dir)
        with zipfile.ZipFile(str(self._wheel)) as zip_ref:
            self._shorten_path_if_needed(zip_ref)
            zip_ref.extractall(str(self._image_dir))
findings.reasoning: build_image() extracts the seed wheel (pip/setuptools/wheel) with zipfile.extractall into the app-data image folder. No pre-validation of member names is performed (extractall's default sanitizer in modern CPython strips absolute paths and '..' components, but on older/patched interpreters or when the wheel contains absolute Windows paths this can still write outside the target directory). The archive origin is the bundled wheel inside the virtualenv zipapp or a wheel cached in the app-data 'house' after being downloaded from PyPI by `acquire.download_wheel` (no hash pinning), so exploitation requires a compromised/poisoned wheel in the app-data house or a malicious bundled wheel. This is a real but low-likelihood supply-chain / traversal risk rather than a directly attacker-controlled one; worth manual review for adding an explicit member-name validation before extraction.

evidence.code_context: build_image() -> zipfile.ZipFile(self._wheel).extractall(str(self._image_dir)); self._wheel comes from the app-data wheel house / bundle (see seed/wheels/acquire.download_wheel and from_bundle).
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Sink: zip_ref.extractall(self._image_dir). Source: wheel path stored in app_data house or bundled wheel; not derived from network data at this point, no hash verification visible in the surrounding code.
evidence.notes: Extraction target is a private per-app-data image directory; extractall sanitizes '..' on supported CPython versions.

def extract(full_path, dest):

    sub_file = _get_path_within_zip(full_path)
    with zipfile.ZipFile(ROOT, "r") as zip_file:

findings.description: TLS certificate verification disabled as fallback context for urlopen to pypi.org metadata endpoint
findings.code_snippet:
def _request_context():
    yield None
    # fallback to non verified HTTPS (the information we request is not sensitive, so fallback)
    yield ssl._create_unverified_context()  # noqa: S323, SLF001
findings.reasoning: `_pypi_get_distribution_info` calls `urlopen(f"https://pypi.org/pypi/{distribution}/json", context=context)` iterating over `_request_context()`, which yields None (verified default) first and then `ssl._create_unverified_context()` on URLError. So the unverified context is only used after a verified attempt fails, i.e. exactly when a MITM is most plausible (or the local CA store is broken). The fetched JSON (`releases[...][upload_time]`) is not confidential, but it feeds `release_date`, which drives the grace-period / version-selection logic in `NewVersion.use()` and thus which pip/setuptools wheel virtualenv installs. An on-path attacker can therefore forge upload dates over a downgraded/unverified connection and influence wheel selection; the wheel bytes themselves are fetched by a separate pip invocation, so this is not full RCE, but it is a real (if low-impact) integrity weakening. Deliberate design decision documented in the comment — reviewer judgement needed on whether falling back to unverified TLS is acceptable.

evidence.code_context: def _request_context(): yield None; yield ssl._create_unverified_context()  ...  for context in _request_context(): with urlopen(url, context=context) as file_handler: content = json.load(file_handler); break

evidence.notes: Only used as a fallback after the verified request fails; no noqa S323 suppression review documented beyond comment.

findings.description: Zip extraction sink is not vulnerable to zip-slip: entry name is replaced with a single basename and source path is validated to be inside the zipapp root
findings.code_snippet:
def extract(full_path, dest):
    LOGGER.debug("extract %s to %s", full_path, dest)
    sub_file = _get_path_within_zip(full_path)
    with zipfile.ZipFile(ROOT, "r") as zip_file:
        info = zip_file.getinfo(sub_file)
        info.filename = dest.name
        zip_file.extract(info, str(dest.parent))
findings.reasoning: The CodeQL query flags `zip_file.extract(info, str(dest.parent))` with "path argument [ControlFlowNode for str()]". However this is not attacker-controlled in a traversal-relevant way: (1) the ZipFile is opened on the constant `ROOT` — the virtualenv zipapp itself, i.e. trusted first-party archive content, not user-supplied archives; (2) `sub_file` is validated by `_get_path_within_zip`, which resolves the path with realpath/abspath and raises RuntimeError unless it starts with `f"{ROOT}{os.sep}"`; (3) crucially, `info.filename` is overwritten with `dest.name`, which is only the final path component (`AppDataDiskFolder.extract` passes `dest = root.path / path.name`). Therefore no zip entry name containing `../` or an absolute path can influence the extraction target — the classic zip-slip precondition is eliminated by design. The extraction root is also a virtualenv-managed app-data folder (`lock / "unzip" / __version__` or user-supplied `to_folder`), not a privileged location. Only real archive members from virtualenv's own .pyz are extracted.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source candidate: `path` (module file path) / archive member names. Sink: zip_file.extract(info, str(dest.parent)). Path validation in _get_path_within_zip restricts source members to inside ROOT (the zipapp). The extracted name is forcibly set to dest.name (a bare basename), so archive-declared names cannot escape dest.parent. No traversal path exists.
evidence.notes: Only reachable when IS_ZIPAPP is true (running virtualenv as a .pyz). Archive is the trusted virtualenv bundle.

findings.description: TLS certificate verification is disabled as an automatic fallback in _pypi_get_distribution_info: when the verified HTTPS request to pypi.org fails, the code silently retries with ssl._create_unverified_context(), allowing a MITM to supply forged PyPI JSON data.
findings.reasoning: The URL is HTTPS (https://pypi.org/pypi/{distribution}/json), so the network traffic is not plaintext; however, `_request_context()` yields `None` first (default, verified context) and then unconditionally yields `ssl._create_unverified_context()` as a fallback. Because the loop retries on any `URLError` — which is exactly what a TLS handshake failure against an attacker-presented (self-signed/invalid) certificate raises — an active network attacker (rogue Wi-Fi, ARP/DNS spoofing, malicious proxy, compromised CDN) can force the client into the unverified path and serve arbitrary JSON for the PyPI metadata. The `# noqa: S323, SLF001` comments show the degradation is deliberate, and the author's justification ("the information we request is not sensitive") is only partly true: the data is not confidential, but its integrity drives virtualenv's wheel-update decision logic. `release_date_for_wheel_path()` parses `content["releases"][wheel.version][0]["upload_time"]` and feeds it into `NewVersion.release_date`, which is used by `NewVersion.use()` to enforce `GRACE_PERIOD_MINOR = 28 days` before a newly released wheel is adopted. Forged data can therefore set an upload date arbitrarily far in the past, bypassing the freshness grace period so a freshly published (potentially compromised/typosquatted) wheel version is activated immediately on subsequent runs. Impact is bounded: the wheel itself is still fetched by `pip download` in a subprocess, which enforces its own certificate verification, and `distribution` comes only from the internal `BUNDLE_SUPPORT` table (no user-controlled URL/host injection), so this is an integrity/timing weakening rather than direct code execution.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Sink: urlopen(url, context=<unverified SSLContext>) at line 353. Source of context: generator _request_context() (lines 333-336) which yields None then ssl._create_unverified_context(); the loop in _pypi_get_distribution_info (lines 349-357) selects the second, certificate-disabled context on any URLError from the first attempt. Consumed data: content -> release_date_for_wheel_path() (line 320-330) -> content["releases"][wheel.version][0]["upload_time"] -> NewVersion(release_date=...) -> NewVersion.use() grace-period comparison (GRACE_PERIOD_MINOR = 28 days).
evidence.notes: URL host is hardcoded (pypi.org); `distribution` originates from the internal BUNDLE_SUPPORT mapping, so no SSRF/host-injection. Only integrity of update-timing metadata is affected; wheel bytes are still verified by pip's own TLS stack. grep for 'ssl' in the file shows only lines 8 and 336 - this is the single unverified-context site.

findings.description: TLS certificate verification disabled via ssl._create_unverified_context() fallback for PyPI metadata fetch
findings.code_snippet:
def _request_context():
    yield None
    # fallback to non verified HTTPS (the information we request is not sensitive, so fallback)
    yield ssl._create_unverified_context()  # noqa: S323, SLF001
findings.reasoning: This is the root-cause location of the insecure network call: `_request_context()` is a two-step generator whose second (fallback) iteration yields an SSL context with certificate verification and hostname checking fully disabled (`ssl._create_unverified_context()`). It is consumed at line 351-353 by `for context in _request_context(): with urlopen(url, context=context)`, meaning any TLS failure (including active MITM attack where the attacker presents an invalid/self-signed certificate) simply triggers a *silent retry over a completely unverified TLS channel*. This defeats the purpose of HTTPS: a network-positioned attacker (rogue Wi-Fi, ARP/DNS spoofing) can intercept/modify the response from `https://pypi.org/pypi/<distribution>/json` and forge release metadata. Because the `urlopen` in the unverified pass reports `content` successfully, no error is logged and the swapped data is trusted.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: distribution (user/CLI controlled wheel distribution name, e.g. 'pip') -> f-string URL https://pypi.org/pypi/{distribution}/json -> urlopen(url, context=context) with context from _request_context() second yield = ssl._create_unverified_context() (CERT_NONE, check_hostname=False) -> json.load -> content used by release_date_for_wheel_path() to decide NewVersion.use() grace periods and which bundled wheel is selected/allowed to be used.

findings.description: TLS certificate verification is disabled as a silent fallback in periodic_update: `ssl._create_unverified_context()` is yielded by `_request_context()` and passed to `urlopen()`, so PyPI metadata (version list / release dates) can be fetched over an unauthenticated HTTPS connection.
findings.reasoning:
`_request_context()` is a two-stage generator: the first iteration yields `None` (default, verifying context), and if that request raises `URLError` (e.g. enterprise proxy / intercepting CA / MITM that forces the verified handshake to fail) the loop continues to the second yield, `ssl._create_unverified_context()`, which has `check_hostname=False` and `verify_mode=CERT_NONE`. That context is then handed directly to `urlopen(url, context=context)` (line 353).

Consequently an active network attacker can deliberately cause the first (verified) request to fail — which downgrades the client into a mode where any TLS certificate is accepted — and then serve arbitrary JSON for `https://pypi.org/pypi/<distribution>/json`. The parsed response data drives real security-relevant decisions downstream:

* `release_date_for_wheel_path()` (line 299/323) reads `content["releases"][wheel.version][0]["upload_time"]` and this becomes `NewVersion.release_date`,
* `NewVersion.use()` (lines 126-137) uses `release_date` to decide whether the 28-day `GRACE_PERIOD_MINOR` / 1h `GRACE_PERIOD_CI` grace periods have elapsed, i.e. whether a newly published wheel is safe enough to install,
* the response also influences which wheel version is selected for download.

This weakens the integrity of the update-selection logic (attacker can shrink/forge release dates to make a freshly-published or downgraded version look old and trusted). The actual wheel bytes are fetched by a separate code path (`acquire.download_wheel`), which limits the impact to metadata/selection manipulation rather than direct arbitrary wheel injection into the same request, and the comment shows the fallback is a deliberate trade-off. Hence severity is low but the flaw (CWE-295 improper certificate validation / CWE-300-adjacent channel weakening) is genuine and reachable in default operation (periodic update is enabled by default in virtualenv).

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source: _request_context() second yield -> ssl._create_unverified_context() (CERT_NONE, check_hostname=False). Sink: urlopen(url, context=context) at line 353, with url = f"https://pypi.org/pypi/{distribution}/json". No validation of the returned JSON, no signature check, no pinning. The result is cached in _PYPI_CACHE and flows into release_date_for_wheel_path -> NewVersion.release_date -> NewVersion.use() grace-period logic which gates whether an updated wheel is adopted.
evidence.notes: `grep_search` confirms `ssl` is imported only for this one unverified context; `# noqa: S323, SLF001` shows the developers knowingly suppressed the bandit/flake8 warning. The fallback triggers on any URLError of the first attempt, which a MITM blocking/invalidating the verified handshake can force deterministically. Additional grep showed only two ssl references and no other certificate-verification configuration in this module, so no compensating control exists. Tests mock `release_date_for_wheel_path` so this path is not covered by CI.

findings.description: TLS certificate verification is silently disabled as a fallback when fetching PyPI release metadata (ssl._create_unverified_context), enabling on-path attackers to spoof pypi.org JSON responses.
findings.code_snippet:
def _request_context():
    yield None
    # fallback to non verified HTTPS (the information we request is not sensitive, so fallback)
    yield ssl._create_unverified_context()  # noqa: S323, SLF001
findings.reasoning:
`_request_context()` is a generator that first yields `None` (default, verified TLS context) and, on any failure of the verified request, yields `ssl._create_unverified_context()`. It is consumed by `_pypi_get_distribution_info()`:

```
for context in _request_context():
    try:
        with urlopen(url, context=context) as file_handler:  # noqa: S310
            content = json.load(file_handler)
        break
    except URLError as exception:
        LOGGER.error(...)
```

Any attacker able to disturb the legitimate verified connection (e.g. an on-path attacker or hostile Wi-Fi/proxy that can hijack/blackhole TLS to pypi.org) forces the `URLError` branch, causing the code to retry with `ssl._create_unverified_context()`. With no certificate validation and no hostname verification, the attacker can present a self-signed cert for pypi.org and return arbitrary JSON. The parsed payload is used by `release_date_for_wheel_path()` → `content["releases"][wheel.version][0]["upload_time"]`, which drives the periodic auto-update grace-period logic (`NewVersion.use()`), i.e. which cached wheel version virtualenv will silently select and install into the target environment. There is no signature/MAC/hash verification of this metadata, so the integrity of update-selection decisions is fully attacker controlled once the fallback path is reached.

Mitigations reducing impact: pip (a separate subprocess in acquire.download_wheel) is responsible for actually fetching wheel artifacts and does perform its own TLS/policy checks, so this metadata alone does not directly deliver arbitrary code. Nevertheless, the code intentionally weakens transport security based on an unverified assumption ("the information we request is not sensitive"), the fallback is automatic rather than opt-in, and the client is trivially forced into it by any network-level interference. Recommendation: remove the unverified fallback (use the default verified context only, or `ssl.create_default_context()` with `check_hostname=True`, `verify_mode=CERT_REQUIRED`), and report update-check failures instead of degrading security.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: ssl._create_unverified_context() (line 336) -> yielded to _pypi_get_distribution_info loop (line ~353) -> urlopen(url, context=context) parses remote JSON unauthenticated -> _PYPI_CACHE -> release_date_for_wheel_path() (line 323/325-327) -> NewVersion(release_date=...) in _run_manual_upgrade/periodic update (line 299) -> NewVersion.use() decides which wheel from the update log is installed into the virtualenv.
evidence.notes: Only sink for this pattern in the repo (grep for ssl._create_unverified_context returned just line 336). No sanitizer/verification of the JSON payload exists (no signature check, no hash pinning of metadata). Upstream marks it noqa S323/SLF001, i.e. a deliberate but security-relevant weakening; exploit requires causing the verified request to fail (trivial for an on-path attacker, e.g. RST/blackhole plus rogue TLS server).
